name: Liam Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, happy to. I spend half my life thinking about this stuff anyway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response in Riverside, the inner-city patch by the old docks: flats, takeaways, a big hospital, a lot of mental health calls. A shift is twelve hours of radio jobs, and if I'm lucky I eat a sandwich in the car. I'm on the force's pilot group for an AI assistant that drafts statements and pulls up a person's history, so I use it every shift and send feedback. My weak spot is talking too much at scenes; my sergeant says I wind people up when I should be calming them down. I love the variety. I hate the hours spent waiting at the hospital with someone in crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be surprised, honestly. But fine, let's say it fizzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the pilot was still worth it, because the time it saves on statements is real. With friends I'd say the hype people got burned. Online I wouldn't bother; arguing about AI on the internet is a waste of an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've put effort into being the AI guy on the team. But my job's completely secure, my pay's good, and I've got about eight months of pay in index funds. The pressures stay the same: long shifts, hospital waits, and me needing to learn to shut up at scenes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and feeding back to the pilot group. I'd book myself onto the de-escalation course in spring, since that's my real weakness. I'd keep putting 400 a month into my index fund, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit deflated. Like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much time does the assistant actually save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About half an hour a shift on a busy night, mostly on statements and checking someone's history. It's not magic; it gets dates wrong now and then. But half an hour saved on statements is half an hour I'm back out on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you need to learn to shut up at scenes. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man in crisis on a bridge last month, and I kept talking at him instead of listening. My sergeant took over and he came down. I went home and couldn't stop thinking about it.

say: I'd say the pilot was **still worth it** for the time saved on statements.
I'd skip **online arguments** about AI as a waste of time.
think: I'd be **disappointed** after putting effort into being the team's AI person.
My job is **secure**, with eight months of pay in index funds.
do: Keep using the **assistant** and giving pilot feedback.
Keep investing **400 a month** in an index fund.
feel: He feels **calm**, slightly deflated, like a party ending early.
S0.quote: Half an hour saved on statements is half an hour I'm back out on the street.
fieldNote: He's candid about his real weakness, **talking too much** at scenes.
A **bridge incident** clearly shook him and shapes his priorities.
He measures AI in **half-hours saved**, not grand claims.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant and sending feedback to the pilot group
Book the de-escalation course in spring
Keep investing 400 a month in an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I expect. I'd be quite at home in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say get on board early, because it's coming either way. I'd offer to show people on the team how to use the tools. I'd be careful not to sound smug about it, because a few of the older lads already roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The officers who can use the tools well will get the interesting jobs: investigations, intelligence, the specialist units. I'm junior and not the sharpest at scenes, but on the tools I'm ahead of people with ten years in. That's an odd advantage to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a set of tested prompts for the common jobs, like shoplifting files and missing person reports, and share them with the team in the first month. I'd sit the detective exam within a year. I'd keep investing, maybe bump it to 600 a month while things look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited. A little guilty about the people who'll struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the people you'd feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The civilian staff who do the case file checks. That's exactly the checking work the tools do. One of them, Sandra, has helped me with files for two years. I'd want to make sure she gets moved somewhere decent, not just dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be careful not to sound smug. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I still need those older officers. They know how to calm a room and I don't yet. If I come across as the kid with the laptop, nobody's going to teach me the people side.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **get on board early**, since it's coming anyway.
I'd offer to **teach the tools** without sounding smug to older officers.
think: Officers good with the tools will get the **specialist jobs**.
I'm **ahead on tools** of people with ten years' experience, an odd advantage.
do: Build and share **tested prompts** for common reports in the first month.
Sit the **detective exam** within a year.
feel: He feels **calm** and a bit excited, with some guilt about others.
S1.quote: If I come across as the kid with the laptop, nobody's going to teach me the people side.
fieldNote: He knows he still needs **older officers** for the people side he lacks.
His guilt focuses on **civilian staff** whose checking work is most exposed.
He'd actively **bring AI** into his team's work, not just use it.

steps.text: Build and share tested AI prompts for shoplifting and missing person reports
Sit the detective exam within a year
Raise index fund investing to 600 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a whole other thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need to know the force's plan now, not in 2027. Publicly I'd say the government needs a proper transition plan. I'd still tell people to learn the tools, but honestly that advice runs out of road pretty quickly here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the detective route I was aiming for is exactly the thinking work that goes in 2028. Investigation, intelligence, files: all of it. What's left is response, the hands-on part, and I'm not great at that yet. So my advantage disappears, and by 2031 the robots can do response too. I'd be 32 with no obvious job in policing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the detective exam and put everything into the people side: the de-escalation course, mental health training, maybe negotiator training if they'd have me. I'd start a side thing on weekends helping small businesses set up AI tools, because I actually know how, and that buys me a second income. I'd move my index fund into cash for a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Properly anxious. Being the one who was ready with AI and still not being ready is a strange feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years I'd have to become good at the hands-on side, fast. Calming people, holding a scene, talking someone off a bridge. If I can do that well by 2031, maybe I'm one of the humans they keep for the hardest calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move your index fund to cash. Isn't that the opposite of what you'd normally do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Normally I'd say stay in, ride it out. But if AGI hits in two years, nobody knows what markets do, and I'd want cash I can see. It's the one place where I'd be cautious.

say: I'd demand the **force's plan** now, not in 2027.
I'd admit that **learn the tools** advice runs out fast here.
think: The **detective route** I wanted is thinking work that goes in 2028.
I'd be **32** with **no obvious job** in policing once robots arrive.
do: Drop the detective exam for **de-escalation** and mental health training.
Start a **weekend side business** setting up AI tools for small firms.
Move the **index fund into cash** for a cushion.
feel: He feels **properly anxious**, ready yet still not ready.
S2.quote: Being the one who was ready with AI and still not being ready is a strange feeling.
fieldNote: His advantage **flips into a gap**, since his strength is thinking work.
He'd bet on the **hardest human calls** in the three-year window.
He turns **cautious** with money only in this scenario.

steps.text: Drop the detective exam and take de-escalation and mental health training
Start a weekend business setting up AI tools for small firms
Move the index fund savings into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. That's tight, but I'd have a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to plan, not panic. At work I'd keep pushing people to learn the tools while we still have time to choose what we become. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could get through the detective exam and do a couple of years of investigation work before 2031. That's useful experience, even if the thinking side goes. And I'd have time to get properly good at the people side, which I'll need after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the detective exam in year one and get into an investigation team. I'd do the de-escalation and mental health courses alongside. Around year three I'd start the side business with AI tools for small firms, so it's running before 2031. I'd keep investing, maybe 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more alert than worried. Five years feels like a sprint I can actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year four compared with year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd be learning. By year four I'd be deciding whether I stay in policing for the hands-on years or go full time on the business. I'd make that call with real numbers, not a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to before choosing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, who ran a small electrical supply shop for thirty years. He knows what it's like to have your own thing. And my sergeant, who'd tell me straight whether I'm any good at the people side yet.

say: I'd say it's time to **plan, not panic**.
I'd push colleagues to **learn the tools** while there's still choice.
think: Five years allows a **detective exam** and some investigation experience first.
I'd have time to master the **people side** I'll need after 2031.
do: Sit the **detective exam** in year one.
Start the **AI side business** around year three.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but alert, like a sprint he can run.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a sprint I can actually run.
fieldNote: He plans a **decision point** in year four using real numbers.
His father's **small shop** makes self-employment feel normal to him.
He treats the two-year window as **experience to bank**, not a destination.

steps.text: Sit the detective exam in year one and join an investigation team
Start the AI set-up business for small firms around year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then I'm pretty relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this right, so people should start now and not leave it to year nine. I'd keep teaching the tools. I wouldn't make it a political thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a whole career stage. I'd be 37 at AGI, maybe a detective sergeant by then. I'd have the people skills sorted, savings built, and a side business tested. I think I'd come out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the detective exam, then a few years in investigations, then look at a sergeant role. I'd keep investing steadily. Around year six I'd start the AI side business, small at first. And I'd keep working on the de-escalation side every year, because that's the part that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even. It feels like a long game I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting complacent, honestly. Ten years feels long, and it's easy to drift. I'd set myself checkpoints, every two years, to see if I'm on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The officers in their forties who'd be just short of their pensions in 2039. And the civilian staff, again. They'd need help, and I'd back the force paying for it.

say: I'd urge people to **start now**, not leave it to year nine.
I'd keep **teaching the tools** and stay out of politics.
think: Ten years is a **whole career stage**, maybe reaching detective sergeant.
I'd have **people skills**, savings and a tested side business by then.
do: Move from **investigations** toward a sergeant role.
Start the **AI side business** around year six.
feel: He feels **calm** and interested, playing a long game.
S4.quote: Ten years feels long, and it's easy to drift. I'd set myself checkpoints, every two years, to see if I'm on track.
fieldNote: His main risk, in his own view, is **complacency**.
He keeps **de-escalation** as the lasting skill across every scenario.

steps.text: Move from investigations toward a detective sergeant role

Keep investing steadily in the index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out the one advantage I've got. What would help is the force telling us now which roles stay human, and paying for proper training in the people side, de-escalation and mental health, for everyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people are good at that a machine isn't. Most officers I know have never thought about it. I hadn't, until that man on the bridge. Calming someone down is the job that's left.

headlineQuote: Calming someone down is the job that's left.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** inner-city response officer on his force's AI pilot group.
He's **pragmatic**, invests in index funds and stays out of politics.
His weak spot is **talking too much** at scenes, which a bridge incident made painfully clear.
In slower worlds his **tool skills** give him an edge toward detective work.
In the **two-year** world that edge vanishes, so he turns to people skills and a side business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it wipes out his one real advantage.
whatWouldHelp: Early word on **which roles stay human**.
Force-funded training in **de-escalation** and mental health for everyone.
